about: LAWS0008 is a compulsory, non-credit induction module for first-year UCL Laws undergraduates, taught in person in the first weeks of Term 1 and graded pass/fail in 2026/27. It combines an Introduction to the Study of Law (pre-course preparation and early lectures on the English legal system and legal skills) with a small-group case study on a social issue, in which students read their first cases, statutes and articles, write a short piece and contribute to a presentation. This guide explains the module and the foundational skills it introduces; it does not invent a syllabus beyond the official description.

notes.body:
Laws' Connections (LAWS0008) is the induction module that every first-year UCL Laws undergraduate takes at the very start of the LLB. It runs in the first weeks of Term 1, is taught in person, and sits alongside the four 30-credit compulsory modules (Contract, Property I, Criminal Law and Public Law).

Key facts from the 2026/27 UCL module catalogue
- Credit value: 0. It does not count towards your degree classification.
- It is still assessed, on a pass/fail basis. The catalogue lists the assessment as 100% "other form of assessment" and does not break it into components.
- It is restricted to Year 1 undergraduates in the Faculty of Laws.

What it is for
The catalogue describes the aims as introducing basic legal structures, core legal concepts and essential legal skills, and showing what legal academics find exciting about studying law. It uses social issues as the starting point for group work, critical and creative thinking, and close reading of cases, academic articles and legislation.

The two elements
- Introduction to the Study of Law: the basic structure of the English legal system and an introduction to legal and study skills. It includes about 10-15 hours of preparation before the course starts and a series of lectures in the first two weeks of term.
- Case studies: in the first two weeks each student takes one case study built around a social issue. The 2026/27 catalogue lists options including climate change, fake news and falsehoods, home and family, homelessness, the 2008 financial crisis, the gig economy and medical accidents. Students read their first cases, statutes, academic articles and policy or government documents, discuss them in tutorial-style groups, write a short piece of work and contribute to a short group presentation.

How the module began (older information)
A UCL teaching and learning case study published in March 2019 described the module's first run in 2018/19. At that time students took two case studies, each taught through five three-hour classes in small groups; the Introduction to Law material was on a pre-arrival Moodle site and was tested by multiple-choice questions; and students were assessed pass/fail in one case study by a presentation, blog or essay, with the chance to retake. The 2026/27 catalogue describes a different format (one case study per student), so treat these 2018/19 details as background only and follow the instructions you are given in 2026/27.

Why it matters even though it carries no credit
- It is your first contact with reading judgments and legislation, which every other Laws module assumes you can do.
- The skills it introduces (finding the ratio of a case, reading a statute closely, building an argument, working in a group) are exactly those tested in the Year 1 exams.
- The case studies show how one social issue cuts across contract, property, crime and public law, which helps you see connections between your modules.

How to prepare
- Complete the pre-course preparation before term begins; do not leave it to the first week.
- Set up access to the online legal databases and learn to find a case by its citation.
- Read actively: for every case, write a short note of the facts, the question, the answer and the reasons.
- Treat the group work seriously: agree roles early and meet deadlines.
- Check the module's Moodle page for the current assessment instructions and deadlines, as the catalogue gives no detail.

notes.h: Introduction to the Study of Law: the English legal system and legal skills
notes.body:
This element introduces the basic structure of the English legal system. The points below are the standard foundations that all first-year law students need.

Sources of law
- Primary legislation: Acts of Parliament, the highest source of domestic law.
- Secondary (delegated) legislation: statutory instruments and other rules made by ministers or other bodies under powers in an Act.
- Case law (common law and equity): principles developed by judges, and judicial interpretation of legislation.
- Retained EU-derived law, now called "assimilated law", and the Human Rights Act 1998, which gives effect to the European Convention on Human Rights.

The court structure (England and Wales)
- The Supreme Court is the final court of appeal for the UK (except Scottish criminal cases). It replaced the Appellate Committee of the House of Lords in 2009.
- The Court of Appeal has a Civil Division and a Criminal Division.
- The High Court has three divisions: King's Bench, Chancery and Family. It hears major civil cases and appeals, and the Administrative Court (part of the King's Bench Division) hears judicial review.
- Trial courts: the Crown Court (serious criminal cases), magistrates' courts (most criminal cases) and the county court (most civil claims).
- The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council hears appeals from some Commonwealth countries and overseas territories; its decisions are normally only persuasive in English courts, although the Board can expressly direct that English courts should follow its decision (Willers v Joyce (No 2) [2016] UKSC 44).

Precedent (stare decisis)
- Lower courts are bound by decisions of higher courts.
- The ratio decidendi is the legal principle necessary for the decision on the material facts; it is binding. Obiter dicta are other statements of law, which are only persuasive.
- The Supreme Court can depart from its own previous decisions when it appears right to do so, under the House of Lords' Practice Statement of 1966.
- The Court of Appeal (Civil Division) is normally bound by its own decisions, subject to the exceptions in Young v Bristol Aeroplane Co [1944] KB 718: where its own decisions conflict, where a decision cannot stand with a later House of Lords or Supreme Court decision, or where a decision was made per incuriam (through lack of care).
- Example: in Ivey v Genting Casinos [2017] UKSC 67 the Supreme Court's new test for dishonesty in criminal law was strictly obiter, because the case was a civil claim. In R v Barton and Booth [2020] EWCA Crim 575 the Court of Appeal nevertheless held it should follow it. This shows why distinguishing ratio from obiter matters.

Interpreting statutes
- The courts look for Parliament's intention, starting with the ordinary meaning of the words in context and the purpose of the provision.
- Traditional "rules" include the literal rule, the golden rule (avoiding absurdity) and the mischief rule from Heydon's Case (1584), now largely absorbed into a purposive approach.
- Parliamentary debates (Hansard) can be used in limited circumstances, where legislation is ambiguous or obscure and a minister's statement is clear (Pepper v Hart [1993] AC 593).

Citations
- Neutral citations identify a judgment by year, court and number, e.g. [2017] UKSC 67 (Supreme Court) or [2020] EWCA Crim 575 (Court of Appeal, Criminal Division).
- Law report citations identify a printed report, e.g. [1993] AC 593 (Appeal Cases).
- Legislation is cited by short title and year, with sections (s), subsections (s1(2)) and paragraphs of schedules (Sch 3 para 2).
- Official free sources include legislation.gov.uk for statutes and the National Archives' Find Case Law service for judgments.

Study skills
- Reading a case: identify the parties, facts, legal question, decision, reasons and any dissent; then decide what the ratio is.
- Answering problem questions: identify the issues, state the law with authority, apply it to the facts, and conclude.
- Answering essay questions: answer the question set, take a clear position and support it with argument and authority.

notes.h: Case studies: reading, group work, writing and presenting
notes.body:
The case study is the heart of Laws' Connections. Instead of starting with a legal subject such as contract or crime, you start with a social problem (for example, homelessness or the gig economy) and ask how law shapes it, causes it or might solve it.

What you will do (2026/27 catalogue)
- Read early cases, statutes, academic articles, and policy and government publications on your issue.
- Discuss ideas in tutorial-style groups.
- Write a short piece of work.
- Contribute to a short group presentation.
The catalogue does not give word limits, formats or criteria, so follow the instructions on Moodle.

Reading primary sources
Cases:
- Start with the headnote or a reliable summary to orient yourself, but always read the judgment itself; the headnote is not the law.
- Note the court and date, and whether the judgment is majority or unanimous.
- Find the key reasoning paragraphs and identify the ratio.
- Record short quotations with paragraph numbers.

Statutes:
- Read the definitions section and the provision in full, including any exceptions.
- Check that the version you are reading is in force on legislation.gov.uk, since it shows amendments and whether provisions have commenced.
- Ask what problem the provision was designed to solve.

Academic articles:
- Read the introduction and conclusion first to find the argument.
- Ask what evidence or reasoning supports it, and whether you agree.

Policy documents:
- Identify who wrote them and for what purpose; government papers and campaign reports may present the evidence differently.

Writing the short piece
- Answer the exact question set.
- Make one clear argument and develop it in short paragraphs.
- Support each point with a source, cited consistently (UCL Laws students commonly use OSCOLA, the Oxford University Standard for the Citation of Legal Authorities; check what is required).
- Distinguish what the law is from what you think it should be.
- Proofread for clarity and accuracy.

Group work and presenting
- Agree roles and internal deadlines at the first meeting.
- Divide the reading, but share notes so everyone understands the whole argument.
- Plan a simple structure: the problem, the relevant law, the evaluation and a conclusion or proposal.
- Rehearse together and keep to time.
- Make sure every member can answer questions on the whole presentation, not only their own part.

Why this approach helps later
Many social problems raise questions in several areas of law at once. Homelessness, for instance, involves housing legislation and public law duties, property rights and leases, and sometimes criminal law. Seeing these links early will help you in essays across your first-year modules.

Academic integrity
Your written work must be your own. Paraphrase in your own words, cite every source, and check UCL's current rules on the use of AI tools in assessments before you start.

questions.q: What is the ratio decidendi of a case?
options: Any statement of law made by the judges in the case
The headnote at the start of the law report
The legal principle necessary for the court's decision on the material facts
The judge's summary of the facts
questions.why: The ratio is the principle on which the decision actually rests, and it binds lower courts. Statements of law that are not necessary for the decision are obiter dicta and only persuasive. The headnote is a summary written by the law reporter, not part of the judgment. A summary of the facts is not a legal principle at all.

questions.q: Which court is normally bound by its own previous decisions, subject to the exceptions in Young v Bristol Aeroplane Co [1944]?
options: The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, whose decisions bind all English courts
questions.why: Young v Bristol Aeroplane sets out when the Court of Appeal can depart from its own decisions. The Supreme Court can depart from its previous decisions under the 1966 Practice Statement. Privy Council decisions are generally only persuasive in English courts. The Crown Court is a trial court whose decisions do not create binding precedent.

questions.q: According to the 2026/27 UCL module catalogue, how is Laws' Connections assessed?
options: It is not assessed at all because it carries no credits
By coursework that counts towards the Contract module mark
By a written examination worth 25% of the first year
questions.why: The catalogue gives the module a credit value of 0 and pass/fail grading. There is no examination listed, and with no credits it cannot count towards the year average. Having no credits does not mean no assessment: the catalogue lists it as assessed. It is a separate module, so its work does not count towards Contract.

questions.q: Explain the difference between ratio decidendi and obiter dicta, and why it matters, using an example.
markScheme: Defines ratio: principle necessary for the decision on the material facts; binding
Defines obiter: other statements of law; persuasive
Example: Ivey v Genting [2017] dishonesty test obiter; followed in Barton and Booth [2020]
Why it matters: determines what binds later courts
questions.modelAnswer: The ratio decidendi is the legal principle that the court needed to reach its decision on the material facts, and it binds lower courts under the doctrine of precedent. Obiter dicta are other statements of law made by the judges, such as comments on hypothetical facts or on points that did not need to be decided; they are persuasive only. The distinction matters because it decides what later courts must follow. For example, in Ivey v Genting Casinos [2017] UKSC 67, a civil case about a casino, the Supreme Court set out a new test for dishonesty in criminal law. Because the case was not a criminal case, that statement was obiter. In R v Barton and Booth [2020] EWCA Crim 575, the Court of Appeal nevertheless held that it should follow the Supreme Court's statement, so Ivey now governs criminal dishonesty.
